strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: multi-frame spatial understanding for MLLMs, moving beyond the dominant single-image setting toward capabilities relevant to robotics and embodied perception.

The proposed MultiSPA data engine is technically meaningful: it uses 3D/4D annotations, camera poses, depth, point-cloud visibility, overlap-balanced view sampling, and tracked 3D points to generate diverse QA supervision across depth, correspondence, camera motion, object motion, and object size tasks.

The dataset and benchmark are broad in answer/reference formats, including visual dots, coordinates, semantic labels, qualitative answers, scalars, coordinates, and vectors. This is a useful expansion over many existing spatial benchmarks that rely heavily on multiple-choice or single-image settings.

The empirical gains on the MultiSPA benchmark are large: the 8B fine-tuned model improves from 20.43 to 56.11 average accuracy and substantially outperforms stronger proprietary systems on this benchmark. Transfer to BLINK spatial subsets is also encouraging, with 84.3 average versus 57.9 for the InternVL-8B base model.
The paper includes helpful analyses beyond the main table, including data/model scaling, multi-task training benefits, standard VQA retention, and a small out-of-distribution robotics demonstration.
weaknesses: The main benchmark is generated by the same pipeline and source datasets as the training data, with held-out scenes but similar task templates and answer conventions. This makes it difficult to separate genuine spatial reasoning from learning the dataset/task distribution, especially because the model is trained to emit extractable backtick-formatted answers.

Absolute performance remains weak on several of the most important quantitative tasks: camera translation vector accuracy is 18.0, object movement vector accuracy is 12.92, and camera translation distance is 42.33. These are central to the paper's claim of robust multi-frame spatial understanding, so the demonstrated capability is still partial.

Most experiments use only two-frame inputs, despite the framing as multi-frame reasoning. The limitation is acknowledged, but it materially narrows the evidence for scalable multi-frame or video-like spatial understanding.

The real-world robotics application is anecdotal: Figure 5 shows a small qualitative example rather than a systematic evaluation with calibrated ground truth, multiple scenes, or downstream robot-learning outcomes. The reward-annotator claim is therefore suggestive rather than well supported.

Baseline comparison has potential fairness and reproducibility issues. Proprietary models are prompted and post-processed with GPT-4 to fit the required answer format, while the proposed model is fine-tuned directly on the benchmark style. More details are needed to ensure output-format failures are not dominating baseline scores.

The paper depends on large-scale generated data, GPT-4o templates, and substantial training compute, but the manuscript does not provide enough concrete release/reproducibility detail in the main text. Some templates and details are deferred to a website, which weakens standalone reproducibility.

Some methodological choices are underjustified, including the 20% relative error threshold for scalar/vector correctness, the 5% image-width coordinate threshold, overlap range selection, and using 3D bounding-box dimensions as object height/width/length without deeper discussion of ambiguities across object orientation and scene annotations.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: multi-frame spatial reasoning for MLLMs, including correspondence, camera motion, object motion, depth, and size estimation.
The proposed MultiSPA data engine is a plausible way to leverage existing 3D/4D datasets with camera poses, depth, and tracked points to generate large-scale QA supervision without manual annotation.
The task formulation is broader than many prior spatial VLM datasets, supporting multiple reference types and answer formats including coordinates, scalars, and vectors.

The main benchmark results show large improvements over the InternVL base model and several proprietary models on the authors' MultiSPA benchmark, with especially strong gains on qualitative correspondence and camera direction tasks.
The paper includes useful ablations on data/model scaling and multi-task training, and reports that standard VQA performance is mostly preserved after fine-tuning.
weaknesses: The central evidence is weakened because the training data and benchmark appear to be generated by the same pipeline, from the same family of source datasets, templates, answer formats, and task definitions. Even with scene-level holdout, this makes it difficult to separate genuine spatial reasoning from adaptation to the authors' synthetic QA distribution.

The quantitative task performance remains low for some of the most important claimed capabilities. Camera translation vector accuracy is only 18%, object movement vector accuracy is 12.92%, and distance estimation is around 40%, yet the paper makes strong claims about robust/generalizable multi-frame reasoning and robotics reward annotation.

The evaluation protocol is not fully convincing. Numeric outputs are judged correct within 20% relative L2 error, coordinate answers within 5% image width, and baseline outputs are post-processed with GPT-4 for format compliance. These choices can materially affect reported accuracy, but there is little sensitivity analysis or discussion of fairness.

The comparison to proprietary and baseline MLLMs is not sufficient to establish the contribution of the dataset/training method. There is no comparison to alternative fine-tuning data, specialized geometry/correspondence/depth models, or hybrid systems that use explicit 3D estimation, despite the tasks being classical geometry problems.

The paper overstates multi-frame scope: most experiments use only two images, and the appendix explicitly lists this as a limitation. Claims about multi-frame spatial understanding would be stronger with evaluation on longer sequences or tasks requiring integration of more than two views.

The BLINK generalization result is helpful but narrow. It covers only selected spatial splits and shows no gain on Spatial Reasoning; the paper lacks broader out-of-distribution tests on real robot videos, outdoor scenes, camera motion datasets, or human-annotated spatial questions.

The robotics evidence is anecdotal. Figure 5 is a qualitative demonstration on newly collected images, not a controlled evaluation with task success, calibration, reward quality, or comparison against established reward annotation methods.

Reproducibility is limited in the manuscript. The full template set is deferred to a website, the 27M dataset is only partially used for training, and important implementation details for data filtering, source splits, prompt variants, and evaluation parsing are not specified enough to reproduce the benchmark faithfully.

Some technical choices are under-justified, such as excluding roll, using object bounding box dimensions as object size ground truth, relying on two images for object size despite framing it as multi-view integration, and using thresholded visibility/overlap heuristics without validation of annotation noise.

The 'emergence' claim is not well supported. It is based on one task/table and could be explained by optimization, capacity, data difficulty, or overfitting effects rather than an emergent spatial ability.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely gap: multi-frame spatial understanding for MLLMs, beyond the single-image focus of much prior spatial VLM work. The task suite is well motivated for robotics and embodied perception, covering depth, correspondence, camera motion, object motion, and object size with varied referencing and output formats.

The proposed MultiSPA data engine is a substantive contribution. It uses existing 3D/4D annotations, backprojection, co-visible points, balanced image-pair sampling, and tracking data to generate large-scale spatial QA pairs. This is technically plausible and more grounded than relying only on monocular pseudo-labels from web images.

The empirical gains are large on the proposed benchmark: the fine-tuned 8B model improves average accuracy from 20.43 to 56.11 and outperforms larger open and proprietary baselines on most subtasks. The improvements are especially compelling for coordinate correspondence, depth value, and camera orientation/translation direction.

The paper includes useful generalization checks beyond the main benchmark. Results on BLINK show strong transfer on visual correspondence, relative depth, and multi-view reasoning, and standard VQA benchmarks suggest the fine-tuning does not catastrophically degrade general VQA ability.

The scalability and multi-task training studies strengthen the case that the dataset is not merely fitting isolated templates: increasing model/data scale improves hard camera-vector prediction, and adding related spatial tasks improves camera/object movement performance.
weaknesses: The main benchmark is generated by the same pipeline and from the same source families as the training data, even though scenes/scenarios are held out. This makes the central results vulnerable to distribution and template alignment effects; the paper would be stronger with a larger independent real-world benchmark or human-curated evaluation.

Some of the hardest quantitative results remain modest despite large relative gains. For example, camera translation vector accuracy is 18.00 and object movement vector accuracy is 12.92 under a 20% relative-error criterion. These results support progress, but not yet robust fine-grained 3D reasoning.

The evaluation protocol has potentially important ambiguities. Baseline outputs are encouraged to guess and then post-processed with GPT-4 to fit answer formats, but the exact prompts, failure handling, and possible effects on different model families are not fully specified. The 20% scalar/vector and 5% image-width coordinate thresholds also warrant sensitivity analysis.

The claimed multi-frame framing is somewhat broader than the experiments: most training and evaluation appear to use two-view settings, and the limitation is acknowledged only in the appendix. This narrows the demonstrated scope relative to phrases such as robust multi-frame spatial understanding.

The robotics/reward-annotator application is interesting but mostly qualitative and based on a small demonstration. It should be treated as a motivating use case rather than strong evidence of downstream robotic utility.

Reproducibility is only partially supported in the manuscript. The appendix provides algorithms and partial templates, but refers to a website for complete templates; release details for the 27M samples, benchmark, generation code, and exact evaluation prompts are not clearly established in the provided text. The training also requires substantial compute, which makes exact reproduction difficult.

The “emergence” claim is preliminary. The evidence comes from one hard visual-correspondence setup across three model sizes, so it is suggestive but not enough to establish an emergent capability rather than ordinary capacity/data scaling.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely gap: multi-frame spatial understanding for MLLMs, beyond the single-image spatial supervision emphasized in prior work. The task taxonomy is broad and useful, covering depth, visual correspondence, camera motion, object motion, and object size with multiple referencing and output formats.

The proposed MultiSPA data pipeline is technically well motivated. It leverages calibrated 3D/4D datasets, point-cloud projection, co-visibility, camera poses, and tracked 3D points to produce metric QA supervision at a scale that would be hard to annotate manually.

The empirical gains on the proposed MultiSPA benchmark are large and consistent across many subtasks. The model improves substantially over the InternVL base model and strong proprietary systems, especially on quantitative multi-frame tasks where existing MLLMs largely fail.

The paper includes useful supporting studies: scaling with data/model capacity, multi-task synergy, held-out evaluation on BLINK and other spatial benchmarks, standard VQA checks for forgetting, and alternative fine-tuning strategies in the appendix.

The manuscript is generally clear, with concrete task definitions, formulas for geometry-based data generation, dataset statistics, and ablations that help readers understand where the improvements come from.
weaknesses: The main benchmark is generated by the same pipeline and largely the same source datasets used for training, with only scene/scenario splits. This supports in-distribution generalization but weakens the claim that the model has broadly acquired real-world multi-frame spatial reasoning rather than fitting the generated QA distribution and dataset biases.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript. The system depends on GPT-4o-generated templates, large-scale preprocessing of ScanNet/TAPVid3D/ADT/Panoptic data, and very large training resources, but the paper does not provide enough detail to know whether the exact dataset, prompts, code, and trained checkpoints will be released.

The quantitative evaluation metric is somewhat permissive and may obscure fine-grained spatial accuracy: scalar/vector predictions count as correct within 20% relative error, and coordinate answers within 5% image width. Reporting continuous error distributions would make the evidence stronger.

The comparison to expert models is not fully convincing. For example, camera-vector comparison to VGGT uses scale normalization because VGGT lacks metric scale, and the paper compresses specialist outputs into the proposed QA metric; this makes the claim of matching specialized 3D models less directly supported.

The emergence claim is under-supported. It is based on one hard visual-correspondence setting and is confounded by changes in model size and possibly visual encoder capacity, so it should be framed as a preliminary scaling observation rather than evidence of emergent spatial ability.

The robotics/reward-annotator demonstration is anecdotal, with only qualitative examples and no systematic robot-task evaluation. It is useful as motivation but does not substantiate the practical robotics claim on its own.

The data generation choices may introduce artifacts: templated language, normalized coordinate conventions, restricted two-frame training, indoor/egocentric dataset biases, overlap thresholds, and synthetic distractor selection could all make the benchmark easier for the trained model than for models not tuned to the format.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: extending MLLM spatial reasoning from single images to paired/multi-frame inputs, including depth, correspondence, camera motion, object motion, and object size.

The proposed MultiSPA data engine is conceptually useful: using existing 3D/4D datasets with camera poses, depth, point clouds, and tracked points is a reasonable way to obtain large-scale spatial QA supervision without manual labeling.

The benchmark covers diverse input references and output formats, going beyond multiple choice to include coordinates, scalar values, and vectors. This is a valuable direction for evaluating spatial perception more realistically than purely qualitative QA.

The experiments show clear in-distribution gains over the InternVL base model on the proposed benchmark, and the paper includes some useful ablations on data scale, trainable parameters, multi-task training, and preservation of general VQA ability.
weaknesses: The main evidence is too tied to the authors' own generated distribution. Training and evaluation are produced by essentially the same pipeline, sources, task formulations, templates, and answer formats, with only held-out scenes/scenarios. This makes it hard to know whether the model learned robust multi-frame spatial reasoning or learned the dataset/task interface and priors.

Several tasks require metric depth, translation, size, or 3D displacement from RGB images without clearly providing calibration, scale, or other information that would make the answer identifiable. Strong performance may therefore reflect dataset regularities and supervision artifacts rather than physically grounded reasoning. The paper does not adequately analyze this ambiguity.

The absolute performance on the most important quantitative multi-frame tasks remains weak in the main setting: camera translation vector is 18.0% and object movement vector is 12.92%, even under a 20% relative-error criterion. This undercuts the stronger claims about precise multi-frame spatial understanding and robotics reward annotation.

The evaluation protocol is not fully convincing. Numeric/vector answers are counted correct under broad tolerances, coordinate matching uses a 5% image-width threshold, and results are reported as accuracy without error distributions, calibration analysis, statistical variation, or sensitivity to small ground-truth magnitudes. These choices can obscure whether predictions are useful in practice.

Comparisons to proprietary MLLMs and expert systems are not very fair or diagnostic. Closed models are asked to produce exact millimeter/normalized-coordinate answers in a task-specific format, sometimes post-processed by GPT-4, while expert comparisons are limited and include choices such as scale normalization for VGGT. The baselines do not establish that the method is competitive with appropriate geometry pipelines.

The external generalization evidence is narrow. BLINK improvements are encouraging, but the paper reports mixed or modest gains on other spatial benchmarks, and the synthetic 3RScan camera-vector result remains low. The robotics section is only a qualitative demonstration, not an evaluated downstream experiment.

The claimed 'emergence' of spatial understanding is weakly supported. The study compares only a few model sizes with confounded changes in vision encoder and LLM size, no repeated runs, and a narrow visual-correspondence setup. The evidence is insufficient for an emergence claim.

Reproducibility is a concern. The work depends on a very large generated dataset, GPT-4o template generation, extensive compute, task-specific regex extraction, GPT-4 post-processing for baselines, and many sampling/splitting details that are only partially specified. The appendix provides simplified snippets rather than enough detail to reproduce the benchmark and training pipeline reliably.

The manuscript sometimes overstates conclusions. Claims such as matching specialized 3D perception models, scalable generalizable perception, and reward-annotator usefulness are stronger than what the presented experiments substantiate.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely gap: most spatial MLLM work is single-image, while many embodied and 3D perception applications require reasoning over multiple frames. Framing the problem around depth, correspondence, camera motion, object motion, and object size is well motivated and useful for the community.

The proposed MultiSPA data pipeline is technically sensible: it leverages datasets with camera poses, depth/point clouds, and temporal 3D tracks; samples image pairs by overlap or motion magnitude; supports multiple reference types; and produces diverse answer formats including coordinates, scalars, and vectors.
The scale and breadth of the dataset are strong. The manuscript reports 27M+ QA samples from 1.1M images and 26 subtasks, which is a substantial contribution beyond the trained model itself.

Empirical results are convincing overall. Multi-SpatialMLLM improves strongly over InternVL, SpatialRGPT, and proprietary MLLMs on the MultiSPA benchmark, especially on quantitative multi-frame tasks where existing MLLMs are near zero.

The evaluation goes beyond the in-domain benchmark: the paper includes BLINK transfer, synthetic 3RScan camera-vector evaluation, standard VQA retention, multi-task synergy, scaling studies, and comparisons to expert models such as VGGT, Depth Anything, and LoFTR.

The paper is generally clear and reproducible at the algorithmic level. It provides data generation equations, benchmark metrics, training details, sample distributions, template examples, and supplementary algorithms for pair sampling, coverage search, and rigid-body segmentation.
weaknesses: The strongest results are on a benchmark generated by the same pipeline and task templates used for training. Although scene splits are held out, this still leaves uncertainty about template, annotation, and metric overfitting; the external evaluations partly address this but are narrower than the main benchmark.

The reported benchmark accuracy uses relatively permissive thresholds for quantitative tasks, such as 20% relative error for scalar/vector answers and 5% image width for coordinates. This is reasonable for noisy MLLM outputs, but it can obscure absolute metric precision, which matters for robotics and geometry applications.

The MultiSPA benchmark has only 300 examples per subtask, so some fine-grained conclusions across 26 subtasks may be statistically fragile. Confidence intervals or repeated sampling would make the claims more robust.

The real-world robotics/reward-annotator evidence is promising but anecdotal. The paper shows qualitative examples and trends, but not a systematic robot-task or reward-model evaluation, so this application claim should be interpreted as exploratory.

The comparison to expert 3D models is useful but not fully apples-to-apples. For example, VGGT requires scale normalization, and the specialized-model comparisons appear in the appendix with limited protocol detail; these results support potential but should not be overstated.

The emergence claim is interesting but preliminary. It is based on one visual-correspondence setting and a small set of model sizes, so it is better viewed as an observation than a well-established phenomenon.

Reproducibility depends on access to large source datasets, GPT-4o template generation, substantial compute, and possibly released generation code/checkpoints. The manuscript describes the pipeline well, but acceptance-level reproducibility would benefit from a clearer release plan and exact data/filtering scripts.
